526.title: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom
526.hook: giaan anjan gur deeaa: the Guru gave the ointment of wisdom and the darkness went (Sukhmani 23)
526.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi begin with a salok picturing the Guru's wisdom as anjan, eye-ointment, that ends the darkness of ignorance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jeea, and your line: everything alive is his. Today the twenty-third ashtpadi begins, and it starts with the eyes.

In many Punjabi homes, there's a small bottle or a little metal pot of surma, a fine dark powder for the eyes. A grandmother might line a baby's eyes with it, or her own, with a thin stick, an old custom across South Asia. People say it cools the eyes and protects them. Gurbani's word for eye-ointment like this is anjan. And the twenty-third ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with the Guru putting anjan on someone's eyes.
screen: `A LITTLE POT OF SURMA.` → `LINED WITH A THIN STICK.` → `ANJAN, FROM THE GURU.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: the Guru gave the ointment of spiritual wisdom, and the darkness of ignorance was destroyed. By God's grace I met the holy one, and Nanak's mind was lit up. Take it in pieces. Giaan is wisdom, especially the kind that knows God. Anjan is the eye-ointment, the kohl or surma. So giaan anjan is wisdom pictured as a balm for the eyes. And notice who applies it: gur deeaa, the Guru gave it. You don't put it on yourself. Then the result: agiaan andher binaas. Agiaan is not-knowing. Andher is darkness. Binaas means destroyed, gone. The darkness isn't argued away; it simply ends, the way a dark room ends when someone opens the shutters. The second line says how: har kirpaa, by God's grace, the seeker met the holy one. And the last word is pargaas: light, the mind lit from within. Look at what ointment actually does. It doesn't add anything new to the world. The trees, the faces, the sky were all there already. It just lets you see them. That's how Sikh teaching often talks about the Guru's wisdom: not information piled on top of life, but clearer eyes for the life already in front of you. Over the next days, the ashtpadi shows what those cleared eyes see.
screen: `GIAAN ANJAN: WISDOM AS EYE-BALM.` · `GUR DEEAA: THE GURU APPLIES IT.` · `THE DARKNESS ENDS, LIKE SHUTTERS OPENING.` · `NOT NEW THINGS: CLEARER EYES.` · then, large: `THE GURU CLEARED MY EYES.`

segments.voice: If you can, cup cool water in your hands and bring it gently to your closed eyes two or three times, then dry them slowly and sit, eyes closed, as the coolness fades. When you're ready, open them slowly and let the first thing you see simply be there. If you pray, say Waheguru as you open your eyes.
Giaan anjan, the eye-ointment of wisdom: the Guru gave it, and the darkness of ignorance was gone.
Your line: the guru cleared my eyes. Nothing new added, only seen. Five hundred twenty-six days, and counting.

527.title: Seeing Him everywhere
527.hook: with cleared eyes, He is seen within and without (Sukhmani 23)
527.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that God is seen within, in the company of the holy, and then in all things; Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn teaches knowing the One within and without.

segments.voice: Yesterday, giaan anjan, and your line: the guru cleared my eyes. The ointment is on; today, what the cleared eyes see.
screen: `GIAAN ANJAN — THE GURU CLEARED MY EYES.`

segments.voice: You can lose your glasses while wearing them. Patting every pocket, checking under the couch cushions, asking the whole house, until someone points at your face. The thing you were searching for was right there, closer than anything else, which is exactly why you couldn't find it. Gurbani makes a similar point, in earnest: the One we go searching for is seen, by cleared eyes, both within and without.
screen: `LOOKING FOR THE GLASSES YOU'RE WEARING.` → `CLOSER THAN ANYTHING.` → `WITHIN AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: The first stanza after the salok begins, in paraphrase: in the company of the holy, I saw God within. God's Name began to taste sweet. All things are held within the One, appearing in many colors. Antar is within, the inner self. The cleared eyes look in first and find God there: antar prabh deethaa, God seen inside. But the stanza doesn't stop at the inner room. It turns outward, to all things and their many colors, all held in the One. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, puts the two directions side by side in a hymn in raag Dhanasari. In paraphrase: why go searching in the forest? God lives in everything, yet stays untouched, and is with you too. Like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror, God dwells within; search in your own heart. Within and without, know the One. That, he says, is the wisdom the Guru gave. Two pictures. You can't see the fragrance in the flower, but it's all through it. You can't pull the reflection out of the mirror, but it's really there. That's how the Gurus speak about God within. And the forest matters too. The hymn speaks to seekers who leave home for the forest to find God, and its answer is gentle: you don't have to go anywhere. Look in, then look around. The same One is in both places.

segments.voice: For the first minute, close your eyes and rest inside, the breath, the heartbeat, the quiet under the thoughts, hunting for nothing. Then open your eyes slowly and look around the room or out the window with the same quiet attention, letting inside and outside sit together. If you pray, say Waheguru once inward, once outward.

528.title: The seer and the seen
528.hook: He is both the one who sees and what is seen (Sukhmani 23)
528.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that God is both the one who sees and what is seen, and teachers explain this both as oneness and as presence within a God who is also beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, antar, and your line: within and without. Today the question turns around: not what the eyes see, but who is seeing.

Point your phone's camera at a mirror. On the screen you'll see the phone, and in the phone's screen a smaller phone, and inside that a smaller one, shrinking into the distance. The camera is looking at itself looking. It's a fun trick for about ten seconds, and then it gets a little dizzying. Who's the watcher, and what's being watched? Sukhmani's twenty-third ashtpadi gives a startling answer: God is both, the seer and the seen.
screen: `A CAMERA FACING A MIRROR.` → `LOOKING AT ITSELF LOOKING.` → `THE SEER AND THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Having cleared the eyes and shown God within and without, the twenty-third ashtpadi takes one more step. In paraphrase: God Himself is the one who sees, and God Himself is what is seen. Gurbani uses this pattern of aap, Himself, often: God Himself the speaker and the listener, the giver and the receiver. In Japji, Guru Nanak says the Creator, having made the world, watches over it. Sukhmani goes a step further: the watching itself, the light in your eyes, comes from God. Here's one way to feel it. Every look has two ends: you, looking, and the thing you look at. Usually we notice only the thing, the tree, the screen, the face, and almost never the looking. Sukhmani says both ends are held by the One. In that picture, the tree is God's play, and the light by which you see it, the jot within, is God's Light too. Drisat is the word for sight or glance. Sikh teachers explain this in more than one way, and it's fair to say so. Some stress oneness: there is finally only God, seeing God. Others stress that God is present in all and yet beyond all, so creature and Creator stay distinct even while the Light is shared. Gurbani holds the mystery without settling it in a slogan. Either way, in Sukhmani's picture, seeing is not a small, private thing; it's lit by the One.

segments.voice: Look at one thing, a cup, a window, your hand, for a few breaths, and then, without looking away, notice the looking itself: that light is reaching you, that something in you is seeing. Rest in both at once, coming back to the cup whenever the mind wanders. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as the light you see by.
Drisat, sight or glance: Sukhmani says God is at both ends of every drisat: the light that sees, and the world that is seen.
Your line: lit by the One. Both ends of every look. Day five hundred twenty-eight, done.

529.title: Living ashtpadi 23
529.hook: clear sight is a gift, not a skill
529.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that clear sight comes by God's grace and the Guru's wisdom, and they keep daily practice as a way of making room for that light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, drisat, and your line: lit by the One. Today the whole twenty-third ashtpadi, the cleared eyes, goes out into the day.

The first week in a new apartment, you notice everything: the way the light hits the kitchen at four o'clock, the creak in the third stair, the neighbor's wind chime. A year later, you walk past all of it without a glance. Nothing changed. The light still comes in at four. You just stopped seeing it. That fading is ordinary, and easy to miss. The twenty-third ashtpadi has something to say about it, from an unexpected direction.
screen: `THE FIRST WEEK: YOU NOTICE EVERYTHING.` → `A YEAR LATER: NOTHING.` → `AN UNEXPECTED ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-third ashtpadi in brief. The Guru applies giaan anjan, the eye-ointment of wisdom, and the darkness of not-knowing ends. With cleared eyes, God is seen within and without, at both ends of every look, the seer and the seen. The natural modern response: great, how do I train my eyes? What's the technique? Sukhmani gently sets that aside. Look again at the salok. Who gave the ointment? The Guru. How did the seeker meet the holy one? Har kirpaa te: by God's grace. Clear sight, in this ashtpadi, isn't a skill you master like a language or a golf swing. It's a gift you receive. That doesn't make practice pointless. Sikh practice still includes amrit vela, the company of the sangat, recitation. One way to picture it: practice is more like opening the shutters than building a lamp. In the salok's picture, the light comes from elsewhere. You can make room for it; you can't manufacture it. And there's real freedom in that. If seeing freshly were a skill, every dull, blurry day would be your failure. If it's a gift, a blurry day is just a day the shutters stuck, and tomorrow the light may come in again. The salok's last word is pargaas, the mind lit up. Not lit by effort; lit, the way a room is when the sun comes through.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: OINTMENT, SIGHT, SEER.` · `HAR KIRPAA TE: BY GOD'S GRACE.` · `OPENING SHUTTERS, NOT BUILDING LAMPS.` · `A BLURRY DAY IS NOT A FAILURE.` · then, large: `SEE FRESHLY.`

segments.voice: Choose something you see every day and never notice, a doorframe, a mug, the view from your usual chair, and look at it as if you'd just moved in: its color, its shape, a scratch, the way light lands on it. Don't force a feeling; leave the shutters open, and if nothing comes in, that's fine too. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look.

530.title: Ashtpadi 24, salok: the perfect Lord
530.hook: pooraa prabh aaraadhiaa: I worshiped the perfect Lord (Sukhmani 24)
530.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the final ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib begin with a salok that names God pooraa, perfect and whole, four times, moving from worship to finding to song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pargaas, and your line: see freshly. Today Sukhmani reaches its last ashtpadi, the twenty-fourth.

Listen to how often you say perfect in a day. The barista asks if oat milk is okay: perfect. A coworker says the meeting moved to three: perfect. A friend is running ten minutes late: perfect. We've worn the word down until it means fine, or got it, or sure. Sukhmani's twenty-fourth ashtpadi opens with that same word, pooraa, four times in two short lines. And it means it, every time.
screen: `OAT MILK? PERFECT.` → `A WORD WORN DOWN TO FINE.` → `POORAA, FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: I worshiped the perfect Lord, whose Name is perfect. Nanak has found the perfect One; sing the praises of the perfect One. Pooraa means full, complete, whole, lacking nothing. A pooraa glass is filled to the top. A pooraa job is finished. When Gurbani calls God pooraa, nothing in God is missing or partial, and nothing needs to be added. Count it as it goes: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised. Like a bell rung four times. And look at the order. First aaraadhiaa: I worshiped, I remembered with devotion. Then paaiaa: I found. Then the invitation, gaau: sing. Worship leads to finding; finding spills over into song. That's the whole of Sukhmani in miniature. It's fitting that this is the last salok. Over twenty-three ashtpadis, Sukhmani has walked through nearly everything a life holds: pride and humility, slander and praise, wealth that stays behind, the wanderer at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment of wisdom. Now it gathers all of that into one word. Not a summary of the argument; a word of praise. After all the teaching, what's left is gratitude, sung. The word we've worn down to fine gets its weight back: full, whole, lacking nothing. In these two short lines, only one thing is called that, four times running.
screen: `POORAA: FULL, WHOLE, LACKING NOTHING.` · `FOUR TIMES, LIKE A BELL.` · `WORSHIP, THEN FINDING, THEN SONG.` · `THE LAST SALOK GATHERS IT ALL.` · then, large: `THE PERFECT ONE.`

segments.voice: Let one thing that's full and good come to mind, a person's kindness, a view, a piece of music, the fact of your own breathing, and stay with it until gratitude rises on its own. Then let it out once, in a single word or phrase, and rest in the quiet after it. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru, itself a word of wonder and praise.
Pooraa, full, perfect, complete: its salok rings pooraa four times: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised.
Your line: the perfect one. Not fine, not okay, but full and lacking nothing. See you tomorrow.

531.title: Perfect is His way
531.hook: perfect is His way and perfect His Word (Sukhmani 24)
531.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's last ashtpadi hear of the perfect Guru, Word and way, and meet hard days with bhaanaa, acceptance of God's will, remembering God with each breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pooraa, and your line: the perfect one. The salok rang it four times. Today: what does a perfect way look like on a day that isn't?

The car won't start. The rain comes in sideways. The email you were waiting for says no. By ten in the morning, the day is clearly not going to be a perfect one. Then Sukhmani's last ashtpadi says something that sounds almost cheeky on a day like that: perfect is His way, and perfect His Word. It isn't saying the car will start. It's saying something about what lies underneath the day that won't.
screen: `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `THE EMAIL SAYS NO.` → `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH?`

segments.voice: The twenty-fourth ashtpadi keeps ringing pooraa, perfect, through its stanzas. Its first stanza begins, in paraphrase: listen to the teaching of the perfect Guru; see the Supreme as near you; remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind will lift. Perfect Guru, perfect Word, perfect way. Here's what perfect is not claiming. It isn't claiming every day will feel perfect, or that bad things don't happen. Sikh history has martyrdoms in it, Gurus among them. The tradition doesn't pretend life is smooth. What it claims is something underneath the surface: that God's hukam, God's order, is whole, even when we only see a ragged piece of it. Sikhs speak of meeting the day that way as bhaanaa mannanaa: accepting bhaanaa, God's will. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, sings in another hymn, in paraphrase: whatever You do seems sweet to me. Sikh tradition remembers that he lived those words to the end. That's the trust this stanza points to. Not pretending the rain isn't sideways; trusting there's a whole beneath the part. And notice the practical line in the middle: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety lifts. Saas saas. The trust isn't one big leap. It's breath by breath, on the imperfect day itself. Perfect underneath, imperfect on top: Sukhmani asks the reciter to live in both.
screen: `THE PERFECT GURU, THE PERFECT WORD.` · `NOT A CLAIM THAT DAYS FEEL PERFECT.` · `BHAANAA: GOD'S WILL, ACCEPTED.` · `SAAS SAAS: BREATH BY BREATH.` · then, large: `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Name to yourself, plainly, what's gone wrong today or this week, without arguing with it. Then, on each breath in, hold the thought, this is the surface, and on each breath out, there's a whole underneath; you don't have to feel the trust, just practice it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath.
Bhaanaa, God's will: Sukhmani says God's order and Word are whole even when our day isn't; Sikhs meet it with bhaanaa, breath by breath.
Your line: perfect, underneath. Breath by breath, even on the sideways-rain days. That's day five hundred thirty-one.

532.title: The ambrosial Name
532.hook: sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam: this jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name (Sukhmani 24)
532.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib pause at its rahao line, which calls the jewel of peace God's ambrosial Name, resting in the minds of devotees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhaanaa, and your line: perfect, underneath. A week ends today: the Guru cleared the eyes, we saw within and without, drisat, learned to see freshly, then met the perfect One. Today, the line the whole bani is named for.

Plenty of books take their title from one line buried inside them. You're reading along, and there on an ordinary page is the phrase from the cover, and suddenly the whole book makes a little more sense. Sukhmani has a line like that. It isn't saved for the end. It's planted near the very beginning, and the bani's name comes from it. As Sukhmani closes, we turn back to it: the ambrosial Name.
screen: `A TITLE ON AN ORDINARY PAGE.` → `PLANTED NEAR THE BEGINNING.` → `THE AMBROSIAL NAME.`

segments.voice: The line comes right after Sukhmani's first stanza, marked rahao, which means pause: the place in a hymn where you stop and take in the center. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the ambrosial Name of God; it rests in the minds of the devotees. Start with the name. Sukh is peace, ease, happiness. Mani can be read as a jewel, so Sukhmani is often called the jewel of peace; some also hear man, the mind, in it: peace of mind. Either way, the line says what that jewel is. Not the poem. The Name. Then amrit. In old Indian stories, amrit is the nectar of immortality, the drink of the gods. In Gurbani it comes up again and again: the amrit vela before dawn, the amrit of the Name, the amrit Sikhs receive at initiation. It means what gives true life, sweet and undying. And the last phrase: bhagat janaa kai man bisraam. Bisraam is rest, a place to stop and lay down a load, like a traveler's inn. The Name is where the devotee's mind comes to rest. One way to read Sukhmani, then: all twenty-four ashtpadis, with their warnings and stories, their stillness and praise, unpack this one line. Pride and humility, wealth and kindness, the wanderer and the beggar, the cleared eyes: each a way into the same rest. Sukhmani's peace is not a mood. It's a Name, remembered.
screen: `RAHAO: THE PAUSE AT THE CENTER.` · `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `AMRIT: WHAT GIVES TRUE LIFE.` · `BISRAAM: WHERE THE MIND RESTS.` · then, large: `THE NAME IS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, let the body grow heavy, and with each breath set down one load, a worry, a task, a conversation, the way a traveler sets down a bag at an inn. If you pray, let the Name, Waheguru, be the place where you set each one down; if you don't, let the breath itself be the resting place.
Amrit, the nectar of immortality: Sukhmani's rahao line says the jewel of peace is God's amrit Name, the place where the devotee's mind finds bisraam, rest.
Your line: the name is peace. A week walked; the bag can come off your shoulder. Five hundred thirty-two days now.
